title: Book One (1805) — Chapter 17
paragraphs: After Anna Mikhaylovna had driven off with her son to visit Count Cyril Vladimirovich Bezukhov, Countess Rostova sat alone for a long time, pressing her handkerchief to her eyes. At last she rang the bell.
"What's the matter with you, my dear?" she said irritably to the maid who had kept her waiting several minutes. "Don't you want to serve me? Then I'll find you another position."

The countess was upset by her friend's sorrow and humiliating poverty, and was therefore in a bad mood—a state that, with her, always expressed itself in calling her maid "my dear" and speaking to her with exaggerated politeness.
"I'm very sorry, ma'am," the maid replied.
"Ask the count to come to me."
The count came waddling in to see his wife, looking somewhat guilty as usual.
"Well, little countess! What a game stew in Madeira sauce we're going to have, my dear! I tried it. The thousand rubles I paid for Taras were well spent. He's worth it!"
He sat down beside his wife, elbows on his knees, running his hands through his gray hair.
"What are your orders, little countess?"
"You see, my dear... What's that mess?" she said, pointing at his waistcoat. "It's the stew, most likely," she added with a smile. "Well, the thing is, Count, I need some money."
Her face turned sad.
"Oh, little countess!"... And the count began fumbling for his pocketbook.
"I need a lot, Count! I need five hundred rubles," and taking out her cambric handkerchief, she began wiping her husband's waistcoat.
"Yes, right away, right away! Hey, who's there?" he called out in a tone used only by people who are certain their summons will be instantly obeyed. "Send Dmitri to me!"
Dmitri, a man from a good family who had been raised in the count's household and now managed all his affairs, stepped quietly into the room.

"This is what I need, my dear fellow," said the count to the respectful young man. "Bring me..." He thought for a moment. "Yes, bring me seven hundred rubles. But make sure you don't bring me tattered, dirty notes like last time—nice clean ones, for the countess."
"Yes, Dmitri, clean ones, please," said the countess with a deep sigh.

"When would you like them, your excellency?" asked Dmitri. "If I may mention... But don't worry," he added quickly, noticing that the count was beginning to breathe hard and fast—always a sign that anger was approaching. "I forgot... Shall I bring them right away?"
"Yes, yes, just so! Bring it. Give it to the countess."
"What a treasure that Dmitri is," the count added with a smile when the young man had gone. "There's never any 'impossible' with him. That's a thing I can't stand! Everything is possible."
"Ah, money, Count, money! What sorrow it causes in this world," said the countess. "But I desperately need this sum."
"You, my little countess, are a well-known spendthrift," said the count, and having kissed his wife's hand, he went back to his study.

When Anna Mikhaylovna returned from Count Bezukhov's, the money—all in clean notes—was lying ready under a handkerchief on the countess's little table. Anna Mikhaylovna could see that something was troubling her friend.
"Well, my dear?" asked the countess.
"Oh, what a terrible state he's in! You wouldn't recognize him, he's so ill! I was only there a few minutes and barely said a word..."
"Annette, for heaven's sake, don't refuse me," the countess began, with a blush that looked very strange on her thin, dignified, elderly face, and she took the money from under the handkerchief.
Anna Mikhaylovna instantly guessed what she intended and bent forward, ready to embrace the countess at the right moment.
"This is for Boris, from me—for his outfit."

Anna Mikhaylovna was already embracing her and weeping. The countess wept too. They wept because they were friends, and because they were kind-hearted, and because they—friends since childhood—had to think about such a base thing as money, and because their youth was over. But those tears were pleasant to them both.
